[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$

$$

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -4 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ -14 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

If we are given the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ how do we find the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}?$
To find $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ we use the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

The diagram below is a commutative diagram that shows how a change of basis works at each step.

![](images/df/dff02d9f46eb7ded23f418765a50dd1971145cd0e585a82beeef1a45812df8a7.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. So algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}.
$$

For instance, if $[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we use this formula to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the formula for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.
$$

**Note:** Alternatively, if we know the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small {\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \to {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}$ from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B},$ we can construct a similar diagram:

![](images/d6/d6cd195ccd42804ea91debabd23563bb0f6903fdd1b5d708b712c75417fff2a9.png)

From this, we can derive the equation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation
